Since mid-2025, finance and tech have shed about 246,000 jobs. Every other industry combined added about 812,000.

That is the first sector-level split in my archive that points the way the exposure studies predicted. The two most AI-exposed white-collar sectors contract while the rest of the economy keeps hiring.

It also squares with the NBER finding of no AI-driven spike for recent graduates. A net gain of roughly 566,000 jobs makes the aggregate look calm, and the shrinking corner disappears inside it.

We'd hold it loosely. The split shows where the change is landing. It can't tell us why. The number worth tracking from here is the gap between those two lines.

Founders. Nobody understands what you’re going through except… every other founder. 

Building an ocean company is a strange kind of lonely. Your sales cycles are measured in years. Your hardware has to survive salt water. Your investors mostly come from software. And the few people who truly understand are scattered across Oslo, Singapore, Boston and Marseille.

I see it every week. Brilliant founders hit the same walls in the same order: de-risking R&D, landing the first industrial contract, hiring a VP Sales, raising an A or a B when the market wants AI multiples.

Same walls. Different companies. No one comparing notes.

That’s why we’re launching Ocean Scalers: small circles of ocean CEOs at the same stage, who don’t compete with each other, meeting every quarter for a year with an experienced facilitator. CEOs only. Open to every ocean CEO, not only the Rypples portfolio.

This isn’t networking. It’s the room where you say what you can’t say to your board, your team or your investors. Then you get honest answers from people who’ve hit the same wall. 

The ocean doesn’t need more prototypes. It needs more companies that scale. Scaling is learned faster together. First circles start in January. 

Applications close 20 November. Link in comments.

Some recruitment organisations really are pretty sh1t with their standards, processes and service.  

I’m not talking Ai or automation or anything overly funky or groundbreaking.  That has its place, for sure. 

I’m not talking revolutionary ‘blue skies thinking’ and market leading serivice lines. They too have their place.  

I’m talking companies that can’t even be arsed to do the absolute basics…. 

- do you reference the candidates to place on behalf of a customer.  To validate capability, but more importantly to speak to a hiring manager in your space.  Who hired this person?  Is it tracked & reported via the CRM. 

- do you meet all your placed candidates and active buying clients regularly to build true relationships?  Is it tracked & reported viw the CRM. 

- do you have a process to regularly monitor the performance of all your contractors you are supplying.  Is it tracked on the CRM and reported. 

- do you always look to backfill every resignation you create by filling a job.  Is it tracked and reported on the CRM.  

- do you even understand how many new contract placements you can make by tracking end dates & people movement.  Is it tracked and built on the CRM. 

- do you track every contractor that finishes for you to their next project? Every time.  Is it on the CRM and reported? 

- do you understand what lifetime value of a candidate (perm or contract) is?  If you don’t understand lifetime value you’re losing bags of cash. 💰 


There’s hundreds of simple processes 👆that executed on every desk, consistently and with quality leads to regular client wins and more placements.  I don’t mean sometimes we do some of this on some desks.  I mean it’s your DNA and it’s lived and breathed.  Without exception.   It’s a standard you own as the leader.  You demand it because it’s your strategy. 

And yes lots of the above can be automated now.  That’s another discussion.  

I’m talking basic stuff thats died and just doesn’t seem to happen anymore.  Lazy? Incompetent?  Can’t be arsed?  Sh1t leadership?  Loose standards?  Too many exceptions to keep average people happy doing what they’ve always done?  Just turn up and accept mediocre performance? Blind to how to actually do it all?  Don’t use your CRM?  

Sharpen up on the basics before you get carried away with Ai and intergalactic strategies.   Lots of performance and sales opportunities are sitting under your nose if you’re prepared to look. 

Over & out.

I wanted to know what UAE start-ups are actually buying when they acquire other companies.

announcements usually say similar things like "accelerated growth" or "strategic synergies", but these tell you remarkably little about what anyone actually bought.

yet, 3 acquisitions in the last year really caught my attention.

first, Ray powerbank sharing.

Installing a powerbank station into a restaurant or hotel or shopping mall is an extremely long and resource intensive process. So in May, Ray acquired the operating assets of its competitor JetCharge, including its hardware, team and contracts covering 100+ locations.

Then take CNTXT AI - the abu dhabi AI company.

in June, it acquired Actualize which specialises in arabic voice AI, including models adapted to regional dialects. What interested me was not necessarily the tech part, it was how CNTXT integrated Actualize's key personnel. Its co founders joined CNTXT as CTO and VP of AI.

And then PopArabia - the music company with capabilities across music publishing, licensing and right managment. 

It acquired Viral Wave - a music distribution business in April. It gave Pop Arabia infrastructure, expertise and relationship to distribute and monetise music across streaming platforms and Youtube.

So - 3 very different companies that all bought 3 very different things:
Ray bought ACCESS
CNTXT AI bought TECHNICAL CAPABILITY
PopArabia bought DISTRIBUTION

none of these things are particularly easy to recreate simply by hiring more people. 

which makes me think about the number of conversations I've had with founders about what they should build next, which capabilities to hire for, or how to accelerate growth.

there is perhaps another question worth asking... 

What would take us 2 years to build, that someone else has already spent 5+ years getting right?

now of course, buying something is much simpler than integrating it. But I think there is a lot of value in Time, Relationships and Mistakes - that you no longer have to accumulate yourself.

📊 More work doesn’t automatically mean more jobs. September’s PMI data shows exactly why.

UK services activity grew for a third month running. The S&P Global Services PMI came in at 52.1. 📈

But services employment fell for the 24th month in a row. 📉

Why the gap? 🤔
💷 Payroll costs
⚙️ Productivity drives
🤖 Greater use of technology, including AI

Construction tells a similar story 🏗️
Its PMI rose from 44.3 to 46.1, the slowest decline in output since January. Yet construction employment fell at its quickest rate in five months.

It’s not all one-way though ✨
🔹 Private-sector permanent vacancies rose for the first time in over two years
🔹 The UK was among the countries reporting increased manufacturing employment

What it means if you’re hiring (or recruiting) 🎯
✅ Growing workloads don’t always lead to permanent headcount
✅ Some clients will go permanent, others temp or contract, and some will try to do more with the same team
✅ The strongest opportunities come from understanding which route each client is taking

The market is improving, but opportunity is becoming more selective. 🔍

Kumo HR — 1153. HRTech Solution

Most HR teams don't have an automation problem. They have an execution problem.
The tools are already there. An ATS here, a payroll engine there, a leave calendar somewhere else. What's missing is the person in the middle: the one who opens each system, pulls the data, spots the conflict, drafts the document and chases the approval. That work never shows up on a feature list, but it eats the week. And the current wave of "AI assistants" hasn't touched it — a copilot that suggests a next step still leaves the step to you.

Kumo HR is built exactly at that point.

Kumo positions itself not as a chatbot layer but as an agentic operating system for HR. Its Agent 2.0 takes a goal in plain language — build a hiring plan, audit our leave this week, run a 360 for engineering — breaks it into a mission, executes each step, and reads what each tool actually returned before deciding what comes next. It parses CVs, contracts and policies rather than just summarising them, and it produces artifacts: hiring plans, job posts, audits, reports, all versioned and reusable.

The control architecture is where it gets interesting for anyone who has been burned by automation. Sensitive actions are confirm-gated — the agent drafts and stops. Every step, tool call and result is logged. Teams can define Skills, so a process taught once runs the same way for everyone afterward.

Underneath sits a full HR platform: people and org, hiring, multi-entity payroll and expenses, performance and 360, leave and time, learning, engagement, documents and e-signature. Employer-of-Record coverage extends to 180+ countries with localised contracts and regulatory tracking. For technical teams, Kumo exposes an Agent API, an MCP server and a TypeScript SDK, so the agent can be embedded into another product or connected to systems already in use.

An independent note. The agentic comparison Kumo publishes — copilot versus agent — is its own qualitative assessment, not a third-party benchmark, and the company says so openly. That transparency is welcome, but it shifts the burden to the buyer: the only meaningful test is running a real mission on your own data and reading the log line by line. Two questions worth asking in a demo. First: when the agent hits an ambiguous case, what exactly does it do — stop, guess, or escalate? Second, for teams operating in Türkiye: local payroll and social security compliance is not on the published country logic, so where does that boundary sit?

This was during a seasonal hiring ramp for Amazon India, when I was running the contract-staffing business at Aasaanjobs / OLX People.

Recruiting thousands of people was one challenge. Making sure the operations could handle that scale was another.

Every person needed to be onboarded, their identity and bank details verified, their salary calculated and paid correctly, and statutory compliance managed. With seasonal hiring came significant attrition, which meant processing exits and full and final settlements alongside thousands of new joiners.

And unlike recruitment, much of this work had to happen again every month.

The only way our systems could keep up was through automation. Our team had built technology to automate onboarding documents, identity and bank-account verification, payroll calculations, compliance processes and much of the repetitive administration across the contract-staffing + Employer-of-Record business.

This allowed our operations team to focus on exceptions and problems that actually needed human intervention, rather than manually processing the same checks for tens of thousands of people.

We were doing this well before today's AI tools became available. But the underlying principle is the same reason I find AI so useful now: automate the repetitive work and give people more time for decisions that need their attention.

One thing that experience taught me is that scaling a business requires much more than increasing headcount or winning new contracts. Your people, processes, technology, compliance, financial controls and operational capacity all need to scale together.

Boards keep asking how many jobs AI will cut.
Citi put a number on a different saving this month. Its tech vendor spend is down 30% in a year.
Yours is probably sitting in your supplier contracts, and your suppliers are keeping it.

Citi has 14,000 engineers on its main AI coding agent. CEO Jane Fraser said last week what that bought: "We've reduced our tech vendor spend by 30% year-over-year as a consequence, and that's still got a long way to run." I read that as bought-in work now done in-house with AI.

MIT's GenAI Divide report saw this last year: "Real gains come from replacing BPOs and external agencies, not cutting internal staff." The ONS found earlier this month that only 6% of UK firms using AI say it has reduced their headcount.

Your suppliers have the same tools, and some are already saying so. Wipro, one of India's biggest IT outsourcers, did no campus hiring in the first half of its financial year, and its HR chief credited its own AI projects. Their cost of doing your work is falling. Your rate probably isn't.

Many mid-market firms buy development, testing, support or content by the hour or by the head. Citi's route of doing that work itself won't suit everyone, but a credible option to bring some in-house gives you leverage.

I sell AI consulting myself, so I'm not doing my own trade any favours. Before your next renewal, I'd still ask each supplier three questions:
1. Which of our tasks do you now do with AI?
2. How much faster are you at them?
3. And why hasn't our rate moved?

Deloitte cuts 170 jobs in Australia, but it’s hiring 500+ elsewhere. Here’s why. 

Deloitte Australia is making about 170 roles redundant, roughly 2% of its ~11,000 non-partner workforce. At the same time, it plans to hire 500+ people for its outsourcing division.

This looks less like a simple cost-cutting story and more like a strategic pivot.

What’s behind it? 

- The $1B target: Deloitte wants to triple its managed services (outsourcing) business to $1 billion in revenue by 2030.

- Shifting client demand: Deloitte says it acted where there has been a “sustained shift in client demand.” Advisory and deals work has been under pressure, while tax, legal and technology work has grown.

- The search for steady revenue: Outsourcing means running back-office functions like finance on long-term contracts. It’s predictable, recurring income, unlike project-based consulting.

- Lower-cost delivery: These services are delivered by a mix of Australian teams and hubs in India.

It’s an industry-wide trend. The Big Four are all moving the same way: 

- PwC Australia is targeting $500M+ in outsourcing revenue by 2030 
- EY Australia already runs a ~$400M-a-year outsourcing business

My takeaway: 

The consulting model is changing. Clients want ongoing, outcome-based services over one-off advisory projects, and AI is pushing firms to rethink which roles they need.

For professionals, the lesson is to stay adaptable and keep building skills in the areas where demand is growing: technology, data, tax and managed services.

What do you think: is outsourcing the future of the Big Four, or are firms trading long-term advisory strength for short-term stability?

Who builds your software: AI or the professional engineer?

The question itself is wrong. The common mistake is choosing between them; the correct move is distributing the roles.

In our plan for building our sales management system, we adopted the hybrid model:

AI builds inside a governed ecosystem against a written specification, while the professional engineer works as the quality line, not the production line: architecture review, execution governance, signing off every phase before delivery, and solving the technical knots AI can't untie.

Three direct results:

1. Cost drops, because you no longer pay for hours of execution — you pay for hours of technical judgment.

2. Intellectual property stays inside your own ecosystem, so no one becomes "essential enough to hold you hostage."

3. The excellent engineer stays, because professionals grow bored of executing and thrive on supervising — a smarter role raises retention.

The governing rule: the specification is a contract for both parties. Whoever builds — machine or human — works against written acceptance criteria, and whoever approves signs before delivery. This turns hiring from a gamble on a personal relationship into measurable architecture.

AI didn't make engineers cheaper. It made the best engineers more valuable.

Did you ever kick yourself for hiring someone who interviewed brilliantly but turned out mediocre on the job?

Andreessen Horowitz just posted a list of hiring tips, and 2 resonate with me in particular – but implementing them isn’t always straightforward.

Here’s the approach I’ve developed over the past decade to simulate practical work with candidates real-time during interviews.

First, avoid theoretical questions. Not: "how would you build a go-to-market plan?" - which invites a textbook answer and management speak.

Instead, get dirty: share a real-life scenario from your team and ask them to sketch a work artefact on a digital whiteboard while you give feedback. How good are they at putting ideas in writing in real-time? Do they accept redirection graciously or get defensive?

Business development roles - have them draft a short term sheet with specific commercials and ballpark pricing. Not a theoretical high-level outline. Ask them to spell out an important contract clause verbatim.

Account management roles - roleplay a difficult client. Can they stay empathetic and firm at the same time, and adjust as you feed them new information?

Product roles – provide an ambiguous scenario and ask them to build an AI prototype on screen-share with key flows and example pricing. Can they triage your signals into what matters vs. noise, and create something practical & realistic?

The pattern you’ll see is that weak executors might be fine outlining concepts, but stumble when it comes to the gory details. The clear red flag is the candidate who hesitates to dive into the little things, struggles to improvise, and retreats to describing how they "would" do it rather than actually trying to do it on the spot.

The one thing your practical interview still can't test is whether someone will sustain momentum: consistent follow-through over weeks, or persistence when things get hard. That's where references have a key place, especially unsolicited ones. They're not always objective or easy to get, but they're indispensable.

I highly recommend spending half your interview time on hands-on scenarios - your decisions will get sharply better. Some candidates are surprised at first ("you want me to come up with an actual marketing headline right now??"), but I’ve found that the strong ones really enjoy it. It gives them a concrete feel for the job that awaits.

775 new companies set up in DIFC in just the first quarter of 2026, up from 478 a year earlier.
 
If you are one of them, the clock started the day you signed.
 
The first 90 days of a new fintech or financial firm in DIFC decide how fast you can launch. And almost every item on the checklist comes back to one thing: people.
 
Here is how we see it.
 
Days 1-30: Get the foundation right
 → Key leadership and the regulated roles the regulator expects to see in place, such as compliance and MLRO
 → Your first core hires: the people who can speak with confidence to the regulator, banks and partners
 → A clear view of the skills you need now, and the ones you can add later
 
Days 31-60: Build the engine
 → Engineering, cloud, data and security talent to build and run your platform
 → AI and automation skills for onboarding, monitoring and risk
 → A hiring plan that does not stop for every new requirement
 
Days 61-90: Get ready to launch
 → Operations, risk and client-facing teams, in place before go-live
 → A governed way to bring in contract and project talent as demand shifts
 → Enough depth that one resignation does not become a launch delay
 
The pattern we see: regulated and senior roles are the hardest to fill, and the cost of a gap is a delayed launch.
 
At Acesoft, we have supported technology and specialist hiring for 16 years. For firms in the UAE, we start with the talent in the UAE first, and go for a global search only when the skill you need requires it. With a talent pool already in place and priority submissions, the first shortlist reaches you faster.

Buying AI is a lot like hiring someone. You can read the CV, sit through the interview and watch a great demo, but you don’t really know how they’ll perform until they’re doing the actual work. By then you’ve already hired them.

We see this everywhere in AI enterprise deployments. The demo goes well and everyone in the room agrees it looks useful. Then nobody wants to sign off on a full rollout based on a demo - it's just too risky

During my IIM days, the summer internship was the best hiring tool around. A highly motivated student worked closely with the team for two or three months, and if the work was good, they left with a final offer. Both sides knew exactly what they were getting.

Outside campus, that model is hard to copy. It’s expensive, it takes months and it doesn’t scale. And if the person left a year later, everything you’d put into them left too.

That's one of the beautiful advantages of AI - A deployment can run the same exercise in weeks. Training, integration, going live and scaling up all happen inside the pilot, so the client is judging real work instead of a demo. Unlike an intern, it doesn’t leave and take the training with it. We now run all our pilots this way, with one narrow use case and one clear way to measure it.

The chart below is a great example. In June, one client started a pilot with us on a single, narrow use case. It proved what it needed to, and they signed an annual contract in August. Usage has more than doubled since the contract, and October is on pace for 2.5x June.

Running pilots this way has given us very strong signals. Customers are more satisfied because they’ve already seen it work. The success metrics are agreed before anything goes live. And by the time a contract is signed, the whole organisation is clear on what the AI is doing and why.

If there’s a painful task your team deals with every day and you’ve wondered whether it can be automated, reach out to Progent.
